title: Jerome in Bethlehem (c. 347–420)
hook: a prickly scholar translates the Bible into everyday Latin

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's sermon line: love, and do what you will. Your carry was love, then do.

A young scholar falls sick with a fever, and dreams he's dragged before the judgment seat. A voice asks who he is. A Christian, he answers. You lie, says the voice. Ciceronianus es, non Christianus. You're a Ciceronian, not a Christian. The scholar is Jerome, and he tells this dream himself in a letter. He loved Cicero's polished Latin and found the plain style of the Bible hard to stomach. Strange, then, that this is the man who spent his later years in Bethlehem putting the Bible into plain Latin for ordinary churchgoers.
screen: `A FEVER AND A DREAM.` → `A CICERONIAN, NOT A CHRISTIAN.` → `THEN, A BIBLE FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Jerome's letters show a brilliant, restless, sharp-tongued scholar, warm with friends and fierce with opponents. Holiness, in his case, didn't come with a soft personality. Second, the problem he was asked to fix. Latin-speaking Christians had Bibles, but the old Latin versions differed from copy to copy. A pope asked Jerome to revise the Gospels, and the work grew from there. Third, the bold step. For the Old Testament, Jerome went back behind the Greek to the Hebrew. In Bethlehem he worked at it, and he says he learned Hebrew from a Jewish teacher who came to him by night. Not everyone was pleased. Augustine wrote to him, worried that a new wording in the book of Jonah had upset a congregation that knew the old one by heart. Familiar words are hard to give up. Fourth, what it became. His translation, along with other parts of the old Latin, came to be called the Vulgate. And here's the thread that reaches you: the Douay-Rheims, the English Bible quoted on this path, was translated from Jerome's Latin. So when you hear "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," you're hearing Jerome, one step removed. In his Latin: In principio erat Verbum. The common tongue, for the common church.
screen: `A SHARP-TONGUED SAINT.` · `THE OLD LATIN COPIES DIFFERED.` · `BACK TO THE HEBREW, IN BETHLEHEM.` · `THE BIBLE IN COMMON LATIN.` · then, large: `IN PRINCIPIO ERAT VERBUM.`

segments.voice: Say the first line of John's Gospel in Jerome's Latin, slowly, even if you've never studied Latin: In principio erat Verbum. In the beginning was the Word. Say the Latin once more and notice which words you can already guess, principio, beginning, verbum, word, or say the verse in another language you speak at home, and let the strange sound slow you down; if you pray, rest on that one line.
Vulgate. Jerome's Latin Bible, revised from the Greek and, in Bethlehem, translated from the Hebrew, for ordinary Latin-speaking churches. Today's word.
Your line: the common tongue. Familiar words can slide past; foreign ones make you listen. Day seven hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Jerome as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of translators and scripture scholars, and the Douay-Rheims English Bible was translated from the Latin Vulgate.

chat.says: What's the Vulgate, and what does it have to do with English Bibles?
options: Jerome's Latin Bible for ordinary churches; the Douay-Rheims was translated from it.
The first Greek New Testament; every English Bible came straight from it.
Jerome's Hebrew Bible, written for scholars in Bethlehem, not for churches.
chat.meaning: Jerome put the Bible into common Latin, going back to the Hebrew for the Old Testament. The Douay-Rheims English Bible was translated from that Latin.

notes: Letter 22.30 dream: Latin 'Ciceronianus es, non Christianus' (some editions have 'mentiris, Ciceronianus es, non Christianus'); confirm. The voice's English is the script's own rendering.
Letter 84.3: Jerome describes learning Hebrew from a Jewish teacher (Baraninas) who came by night; confirm reference.
Augustine Letter 71.5: the congregation at Oea upset over Jerome's word for the plant in Jonah 4:6; confirm, and that the paraphrase ('upset a congregation that knew the old one') is fair.
Pope Damasus asking Jerome to revise the Gospels: from Jerome's preface to the Gospels; confirm.

Etymology of 'Vulgate' is attributed ('usually explained from the Latin for common'); confirm. The voice says the Vulgate combined Jerome's work 'along with other parts of the old Latin' (e.g., some books were not newly translated by Jerome); confirm wording.
A line on the Vulgate as the Latin Church's Bible for centuries was cut under the claims rule.

Editor pass: hook no longer says Jerome translated 'the whole Bible' (the teach rightly says the Vulgate includes older Latin parts); cut the etymology of 'Vulgate' from voice, trapdoor and original note under the claims rule; softened 'the Latin ordinary people actually used'.
Second editor pass: cut the duration 'for years' (not in the cited letters) and the ranking 'even for better ones' after the Jonah story.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): the word segment and trapdoor floor 2 said the whole Vulgate was made in Bethlehem; the Gospel revision for Pope Damasus was done in Rome (c. 382–384), the Hebrew translations in Bethlehem. Trapdoor floor 3 repeated floor 2; replaced with the Psalter detail (the Vulgate kept Jerome's Gallican Psalter, revised from the Greek, not his translation from the Hebrew; the Douay-Rheims Psalms follow it). Keeper: confirm.
